newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris to decide new BoF council members on Jan 3.
newsitem.headline: Paris to decide new BoF council members on Jan 3.

text.p: The French government is expected to decide on January 3 on replacements for two members of the Bank of France's monetary policy council (CPM) whose mandate expires in early January, council member Paul Marchelli said on Thursday.
Marchelli told Reuters that the council, which met earlier on Thursday, had given its opinion on a list of six candidates proposed for the posts.
He declined to say what was the council's opinion. The CPM gives an opinion on new council members in a purely advisory capacity ahead of a decision by the French cabinet.
The cabinet is next due to meet on January 3.

Two members of the council, ex-journalist Jean Boissonnat and ex-banker Bruno de Maulde -- given three-year terms when the council first met on January 7, 1994, after the central bank became indpendent -- have their mandates coming up for renewal.

Both are believed to form part of a six-to-three majority in favour of the current policy of maintaining a premium of French interest rates over German rates to maintain the stability of the franc against the mark.
Of the two, only Boissonnat is seeking to stay on.

He is included on a list of six nominees which also includes diplomat Pierre Achard, Alain Prate, former vice-president of the European Investment Bank (EIB), Robert Pelletier, former managing director of the Association of Credit Establishments (Afec), Pierre Guillen, ex-head of the CNPF employers' federation, and Jean-Rene Bernard, formerly head of of regional bank CIC, sources close to the nomination process say.

One source said he believed French President Jacques Chirac had intervened to get Guillen and Bernard on the list of nominees. Both are close to the President and, some say, may tip the balance in favour of a faster pace of rate cuts.

The make-up of the nine-member monetary council is being closely watched by financial markets for any softening in the independent central bank's tough line on defending the stability of the franc against the mark.

Sources close to the nomination process say, however, that Chirac, who earlier this month restated his commitment to a stable franc, was not expected to try to push the Bank into any radical departure from that policy.
